title: The Clausius–Clapeyron Equation
short: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) links vapor pressure to temperature.
trouble: Students use Celsius temperatures, or combine ΔH in kJ/mol with R in J/(mol·K).

blocks.html: The table in Vapor Pressure and Boiling shows water's vapor pressure climbing faster and faster as it warms. The Clausius–Clapeyron equation turns that curve into a straight line and lets you predict vapor pressures and boiling points from two numbers. It uses The Number e and Continuous Growth and the properties of logarithms.

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$ with temperatures in kelvins, $R = 8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)}$ and $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ in J/mol. Equivalently, a graph of $\ln P$ against $1/T$ is a straight line with slope $-\Delta H_\text{vap}/R$.

To escape, a molecule needs at least about $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ per mole of energy. The share of molecules with that much energy grows like $e^{-\Delta H_\text{vap}/RT}$ (the same Boltzmann factor behind the speed distributions you will meet with gases). Vapor pressure is proportional to that share, so $P = Ae^{-\Delta H_\text{vap}/RT}$, and taking logarithms gives $\ln P = \ln A - \dfrac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T}$, a line in $1/T$. Writing it for two temperatures and subtracting removes the unknown $A$ and gives the equation above. (It assumes $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ stays constant, a good approximation over a modest range.)

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Water: $\ln P$ (P in mmHg) against $1000/T$. The measured points at 100, 80, 60 and 40 °C lie close to a straight line whose slope gives $\Delta H_\text{vap} \approx 41\ \text{kJ/mol}$.

blocks.title: Vapor pressure at another temperature
blocks.q: Water's vapor pressure is $760\ \text{mmHg}$ at $100.0^\circ\text{C}$, and $\Delta H_\text{vap} = 40.7\ \text{kJ/mol}$. Estimate its vapor pressure at $80.0^\circ\text{C}$.
steps: $P_2 = 760\,e^{-0.743} = 362\ \text{mmHg}$. (Measured: 355 mmHg; $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ is not quite constant.)

blocks.title: Finding the enthalpy of vaporization
blocks.q: A liquid has a vapor pressure of $100.0\ \text{mmHg}$ at $25.0^\circ\text{C}$ and $400.0\ \text{mmHg}$ at $60.0^\circ\text{C}$. Find $\Delta H_\text{vap}$.

blocks.title: A boiling point at lower pressure
blocks.q: At what temperature does water boil when the pressure is $0.700\ \text{atm}$? ($\Delta H_\text{vap} = 40.7\ \text{kJ/mol}$; normal boiling point $373.15\ \text{K}$.)
steps: At the new boiling point, $P_2 = 0.700\ \text{atm}$; $P_1 = 1.000\ \text{atm}$ at $373.15\ \text{K}$.

blocks.html: Using Celsius temperatures, or mixing kJ/mol with $R$ in J/(mol·K). $1/80 - 1/100$ is a completely different number from $1/353.15 - 1/373.15$, and $40.7$ in place of $40{,}700$ makes the exponent 1000 times too small. Check: before you compute, write every $T$ in kelvins and $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ in J/mol. A sensible answer has $P_2 > P_1$ when $T_2 > T_1$.
With calculus: the equation comes from integrating $\dfrac{d\ln P}{dT} = \dfrac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{RT^2}$, a separable differential equation (Separable Equations).
